title: Do penguin species differ in flipper length?
text:
Code: read the data and compute the numbers
library(tidyverse)

penguins <- read_csv("../data/example/penguins.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Mean flipper length per species (2 penguins have no measurement)
flipper_means <- penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(mean_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm))

mean_of <- function(sp) flipper_means %>% filter(species == sp) %>% pull(mean_mm)
gentoo_vs_chinstrap_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Chinstrap")
gentoo_vs_adelie_mm <- mean_of("Gentoo") - mean_of("Adelie")

n_penguins <- nrow(penguins)
n_islands <- n_distinct(penguins$island)
n_no_flipper <- sum(is.na(penguins$flipper_length_mm))
first_year <- min(penguins$year)
last_year <- max(penguins$year)




Code: make the figure
set.seed(3901)  # same jitter on every render
penguins %>%
  filter(!is.na(flipper_length_mm)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.5) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Figure 1: Flipper length by species. Each point is one penguin; each box shows the middle half of a species, and the line inside it is the median.





Finding. Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers, on average about 21 mm longer than Chinstrap and 27 mm longer than Adelie penguins.
Limitation. These are 344 penguins measured on 3 islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica, in 2007–2009; 2 have no flipper measurement.
Data source. Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data (R package). https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/ License: CC0.

title: Guided Project: Statistical Transformations and Coordinate Systems
text:
Part A · Fairness
My group: education. My outcome: income
Question A: “Of each education level, what share has income greater than $50000?” Question B: “Of everyone with an income greater than $50000, what share is each education level?”

A0 · My group and my outcome

a_data <- fairness %>%
  mutate(
    group = education,
    has_outcome = income == ">50K"
  )

a_data %>%
  count(group, has_outcome) %>%
  print(n = Inf)

# A tibble: 31 × 3
   group        has_outcome     n
   <chr>        <lgl>       <int>
 1 10th         FALSE         129
 2 10th         TRUE            6
 3 11th         FALSE         160
 4 11th         TRUE            8

 6 12th         TRUE            4

24 HS-grad      TRUE          264

26 Masters      TRUE          149

28 Prof-school  FALSE          24

30 Some-college FALSE         884
31 Some-college TRUE          215




A1 · The rate within each group (question A)

a1 <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the group", y = NULL, fill = "Has the outcome")

show_plot(a1)



{#fig-a1 fig-alt=’ The plot compares the proportion of people earning over $50,000 across education levels.’ width=672}




WRITE (2–3 sentences):My prediction was that people with higher education levels would have higher income rates. The plot shows that prof-school has the highest income rate, followed by Doctors and Masters. Preschool has the lowest, and most of the 1st-12th grades are about the same level at less than 10%. Since each bar represents a proportion of its own group, education levels with different numbers of people can be compared fairly (except for the ones with low sample sizes, like preschool). ### A2 · Rates with their standard error

a2_rates <- a_data %>%
  drop_na(has_outcome) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n)
  )

a2 <- ggplot(a2_rates,
             aes(x = rate, y = group,
                 xmin = rate - se,
                 xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  # Many groups, and the labels touch the points? Keep every group, and use
  # vjust = -0.8, size = 3 instead of nudge_y = 0.3.
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Rate (share of the group with the outcome)", y = NULL)

show_plot(a2)



{#fig-a2 fig-alt=’ The plot compares income rates across education levels with standard-error ranges and group sample sizes.’ width=672}




WRITE (2–3 sentences): The Doctorate group has the widest standard-error range, with an SE of 0.0584 and a sample size of 61. A wide range indicates greater uncertainty in the estimated income rate, especially for groups with smaller sample sizes. The plot keeps smaller groups visible by displaying every education group, including those with very few observations, rather than excluding them.


A3 · Zoom or filter?

a3_table <- a_data %>%
  count(group) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
a3_table

# A tibble: 16 × 2
   group            n
   <chr>        <int>
 1 HS-grad       1621
 2 Some-college  1099
 3 Bachelors      858
 4 Masters        266
 5 Assoc-voc      220
 6 11th           168

10 7th-8th         82
11 9th             75
12 12th            70
13 Doctorate       61
14 5th-6th         59
15 1st-4th         22
16 Preschool        6

a3_start <- 5

a3_counts <- ggplot(a_data, aes(y = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL)

a3_zoom <- a3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)), expand = FALSE)

# A warning about removed rows here is expected (Session 2, slide 5).
a3_filter <- a3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(a3_start, max(a3_table$n)))

# Lie Factor (Tufte, 2001, p. 57) of the zoomed plot, largest vs smallest
# group: how many times the picture exaggerates the difference.
a3_largest <- max(a3_table$n)
a3_smallest <- min(a3_table$n)
a3_lie_factor <-
  ((a3_largest - a3_start) / (a3_smallest - a3_start)) /
  (a3_largest / a3_smallest)
a3_lie_factor

[1] 5.981493

show_plot(a3_counts)
show_plot(a3_zoom)
show_plot(a3_filter)











(a) From 0











(b) Zoomed











(c) Filtered







Figure 1: Counts per group: from 0, zoomed and filtered.




The zoomed plot’s Lie Factor (largest vs smallest group) is 6.
WRITE (3–4 sentences): What does each version show and hide? Explain the Lie Factor in your own words. Which version would you publish, and why?


A4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome (question B)

a4_shares <- a_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

a4 <- ggplot(a4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of everyone with the outcome", y = NULL)

show_plot(a4)



{#fig-a4 fig-alt=’ This plot shows each education group's share of people earning more than $50K.’ width=672}




WRITE (2–3 sentences): Question A and B point in a similar direction since education levels with higher income rates contribute more people earning over $50000. However, question B depends on the number of people belonging to each educational group. Bachelor degrees account for the largest share of everyone earning more than 50000 dollars, at about 27.2%, followed by HS-grad at 22.1%.

B2 · A mean with its two spreads

b2_summary <- b_data %>%
  drop_na(value) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(value),
    sd = sd(value),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )

b2 <- ggplot(b2_summary,
             aes(x = mean, y = group,
                 xmin = mean - se,
                 xmax = mean + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Mean finishing time (minutes)",
       y = NULL)

show_plot(b2)

b3_start <- 4

b3_counts <- ggplot(b_data, aes(y = group)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(x = "Count", y = NULL)


b3_zoom <- b3_counts +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(b3_start, max(b3_table$n)),
    expand = FALSE
  )

b3_filter <- b3_counts +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(b3_start, max(b3_table$n))
  )


b3_lie_factor <-
  ((max(b3_table$n) - b3_start) / (min(b3_table$n) - b3_start)) /
  (max(b3_table$n) / min(b3_table$n))

Figure 2: Counts per group: zoomed and filtered.




WRITE (2–3 sentences): The zoomed plot makes differences between age-group counts appear much larger than they actually are. The filtered plot removes the smallest groups, making the remaining groups easier to compare but hiding information about the excluded groups. The Lie Factor of approximately 5 indicates that the zoomed visualization exaggerates apparent differences by about five times. I would prefer the plot starting at zero because it communicates the differences in group sizes more honestly.


B4 · Each group’s share of everyone with the outcome

b4_shares <- b_data %>%
  filter(has_outcome) %>%
  count(group) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))

b4 <- ggplot(b4_shares, aes(x = share, y = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of everyone with the outcome",
       y = NULL)

show_plot(b4)



{#fig-b4 fig-alt=’ The plot shows the share of all top-100 finishers belonging to each age group.’ width=672}




WRITE (2 sentences): The 18–39 age group accounts for approximately 93% of everyone who finished in the top 100, while the 40–44 age group accounts for approximately 7%. This is different from B1 because B1 measures the rate within each age group, while B4 measures each group’s contribution to the overall top-100 population.
